Definition: Any material that meets one of the following conditions: 1) Recovered from space, 2) Extraterrestrial in origin, 3) Paragenetically linked to a material that meets condition 1 or 2 or occurs as a direct product of some process involving an astromaterial.
A physical object that belongs to a museum collection.

A collection object comprised of one or more discernible parts, called constituent parts, unified by physical attachment. The object's identity is determined by its constituent parts, which are distinguished from one another within a specific context.
A conceptual data model in which a single physical object, a compound specimen, is composed of and defined by its constituent parts.
Physically discernible and proximal parts of a compound specimen identified by a single determination based on physical and chemical exclusivity relative to the parent specimen.
Notes: A constituent part belongs to one and only one constituent part type and defined in terms of role and proportion relative to the parent compound specimen.

Definition: Refers to the qualitative or quantitative representation of the abundance of a Constituent Part within a parent Compound Specimen.

A described uni-directional association between two constituent parts, a source and target, within the scope of the parent compound specimen. A relation is defined from the perspective of the source constituent part and described using a relation predicate.
Notes: One constituent part may be associated with multiple constituent part relations in either role. Each constituent part relation only exists between the two member constituent parts.

Definition: A term from a controlled vocabulary to describe the constituent part relation

Specifies the relationship between a Constituent Part and its parent compound specimen. Roles are dependent upon both the part and parent object. For instance, a rock (constituent part type) within the parent specimen plays the role of clast and is dependent on both the constituent part and the parent specimen for its existence.

A continuant is an entity that persists, endures, or continues to exist through time while maintaining its identity. Continuants can preserve their identity even while gaining and losing material parts.

The identity of a specimen represented by a name based on formal criteria evaluated by a domain expert. In biological collections, the determination is represented by a taxonomic classification, primarily a genus and species (e.g., Vulpes vulpes, Accipiter cooperii). In the geosciences domain, examples of determination include Almandine, Granite, and Plantae.
Any remains, trace, or imprint of a plant or animal preserved in the Earth's crust since some past geologic or prehistoric time; loosely, any evidence of past life.

An amount of matter primarily (dominantly) having parts created by geologic processes and can include minor parts that are not of geologic origin, such as organic material, and can be solid, fluid, or a mix
A perceived association between two geologic materials described by a relation predicate.

An amount of matter primarily having parts created by geologic processes and composed of one or more Constituent Parts unified by physical attachment. Geologic Objects may include minor parts not of geologic origin, such as organic material or synthetic material generated as a close approximation.
Source: Garcia et al. (2019) and Brodaric & Richard (2021)

Definition: A collection object comprised in part of geologic material
An entity that exists in full during the length of time of its existence, persists through this time while maintaining its identity and has no temporal parts.
A naturally occurring element or chemical compound that is normally crystalline and formed due to geological processes

An amount of amorphous material; commonly the product of rapid cooling of melted material. Includes natural glasses in Earth and extraterrestrial material, some biogenic mineral products, and anthromophomorphic manufactured material.
An object aggregate that has as member parts a material sample that is located in a museum as a result of a process of curation.

An object is a maximal causally unified material entity, meaning b is a material entity which is such that its material parts are tied together in such a way that, in environments typical for entities of the type in question
A material entity consisting exactly of a plurality of objects as continuant (member) parts at all times at which the object aggregate exists.

Designates an aggregated group of tangible objects with a focal characteristic assembled and maintained by an individual or organization over time. A collection comprises multiple items that are conceptually or physically arranged together for a specific purpose and audience, according to a collection plan
Items of a material nature that are units for documentation and have physical boundaries that separate them completely in an objective way from other objects.
The term describing the nature of the relationship between two constituent parts within the scope of a compound specimen
A consolidated or unconsolidated aggregate of mineral grains consisting of one or more mineral species and having some degree of chemical and mineralogic constancy
A collection object identified by a single determination without discernible parts.
The conceptual model for the digital representation of physical specimens where each entity is  characterized by one and only one determination without any discrenible parts.
A term describing the role played by the source constituent part in a constituent part relation
A term describing the role played by the target constituent part in a constituent part relation
Unconsolidated earth material is an 'earth material' that is constituted by an aggregate of solid particles but is not consolidated into a 'rock' it self.

A value belonging to a top-level, generalized categorization scheme for constituent parts where each constituent part belongs to and only one constituent part type. For any given collection, these constituent part types should comprehensively account for all parts found across every specimen in that collection.
Temporal boundaries defined with reference to some geologic evidence such as, for instance, fossil appearance/disappearance or significant change in local rock lithology.

An interpretation made by a geologist of the age of a specimen made by statistical analysis of a single collection of observations. A specimen may have multiple geochronological interpretations made on it, each related to a different observation collection.
A specialized time ordinal interval used to subdivide geologic time based on a corresponding chronostratigraphic unit.

The science of determining absolute ages of geological events and Earth materials. The primary technique utilizes radioactive isotopes and the production and accumulation of radiogenic daughter isotopes naturally present on Earth. It can be applied to various samples, including rocks, minerals, and biological materials.
An identifiable event during which one or more geologic processes act to modify geologic entities.
A natural process that affects the geologic record by acting upon one geologic entity to produce another geologic entity at a later time.
Source: Neuendorf et al. (2005), Richard et al. (2007)

Definition: A temporal reference system that subdivides all the time since Earth formed into named intervals (units) of abstract time and subdivides all the rocks formed since Earth formed into the successions of rock formed during each particular interval of time
The length of time over which half the atoms of radioactive isotopes decay. The half-life remains constant as the number of atoms is reduced, resulting in an exponential rate of decay

The age of a geologic event that resulted in the formation of a geologic material that is expressed numerically and based on the results of a dating technique such as radiometric dating or dendrochronology.
The maximum limit or latest point in time allowed for a specific event, process, or condition to occur or be considered within a given context or timescale.
Notes: Equivalent to time:startTime and oldest age

Definition: The process where an unstable parent isotope loses particles from its atomic nucleus (decay) to form a daughter isotope (product) at a constant rate
Geologic age expressed in years determined by quantitatively measuring radioactive elements and their decay products
Proper chronological placement of a feature, object, or happening in the geologic time scale without reference to its absolute age.
A family of geologic timescales based on the strata and fossil record observed in a specific area, typically at the country or regional level.
The geologic age of a fossil organism, rock, or geologic feature or event defined relative to other organisms, rocks, or features or events rather than in terms of years.
Proper chronological placement of a feature, object, or happening in the geologic time scale without reference to its absolute age.
A temporal system where time positions are measurements expressed numerically on a scale
An ordered system of named intervals
Notes: Each interval belongs to a rank in a mono-hierarchical structure where each parent is divided into one or many children of the next finer rank. This structure allows the set of temporal positions are uniquely ordered relative to the reference system.

Definition: A temporal entity with an extent or duration
A named or identified interval from a temporal ordinal reference system
The lower limit or earliest point in time allowed for a specific event, process, or condition to occur or be considered within a given context or timescale.
Notes: Equivalent to time:endTime and youngest age

Definition: Physical conditions found on the Earth's surface, which are determined by factors such as climate, tectonics, physiography, geography and within the Earth's interior, determined by pressure, temperature, chemical environment, and tectonics.
The physical setting within which a Geologic Event takes place.
A physical or conceptual feature that is hypothesized to exist coherently in the Earth and that results from geological processes.
A pattern in a rock body (foliation, fold) or a feature occurring between rock bodies (contact, fracture).
A broad area in which similar igneous rocks are formed during the same period of igneous activity.

A region in which all parts are similar in geologic structure and climate and which has consequently had a unified geomorphic history; a region whose pattern of relief features or landforms differs significantly from adjacent regions
Any large area or region considered as a whole, all parts characterized by similar features or a history differing significantly from adjacent areas.

An open or surface mineral working, usually for extracting building stone, such as slate, limestone, etc. It is distinguished from a mine because a quarry usually is open at the top and front, and, in ordinary use of the term, by the character of the material extracted.

Groups of provinces linked by a common tectonic history are designated tectonic provinces. Tectonic provinces may contain a collection of sedimentary, igneous, structural, metamorphic, and metallogenic provinces.
A geologic event environment defined by relationships to tectonic plates on or in the Earth.

A fault-bounded area or region with different layers, rock structures, and geologic history from nearby areas that are not connected to them by unconformable contacts or changes in the rock's surface.

A work for excavating minerals using pits, shafts, levels, tunnels, etc., as opposed to a quarry, where the whole excavation is open. In general, the existence of a mine is determined by the mode in which the mineral is obtained, not by its chemical or geological character. The term also includes only excavations for their minerals or valuable mineral deposits.
Unit of knowledge created by a unique combination of characteristics
An abstract model or representation of data for a particular domain or field of study, independent of any specific software or information system.
Graphical and/or lexical representation of data, specifying their properties, structure, and interrelationships
A data model that includes all entities and the relationships among them based on the structures identified in a conceptual data model and that specifies all attributes for each entity.
A simplified representation or abstraction of a system, process, or concept
Specification of concrete or abstract things, and the relationships among them, in a prescribed domain of knowledge
A technical representation detailing how data is physically organized and constrained within a database system, focusing on tables, columns, and constraints rather than entities and attributes.
Source: Agile Data Warehousing for the Enterprise, 2016

Definition: Ability for data shared by systems to be understood at the level of fully defined domain concepts
An alternate lexical label to the preferred term for an entity.
Notes: Alternate names are informal and unregulated by an authoritative body such as the International Mineralogical Association.

Definition: Identifies the entity responsible for assigning and maintaining a formalized classification system
Activity involving grouping similar or related things together; separating dissimilar or unrelated things; and arranging the resulting groups in a logical and helpful sequence
Encoded classification of an object represented by a graphical symbol that conforms to an encoding scheme defined as part of the classification scheme
Notes: Dana Number, Linnaean Taxonomy does not use a classification code, rather just a single latin term

Definition: A stratified tier comprised of nodes with a shared level of granularity in a hierarchy. The distance of a level from the root is expressed as the Depth. The identifier (label) assigned to a level is referred to as the Rank.
A formalized name belonging to a classification system maintained by an authoritative body.
An identifier assigned to a classification level commonly expressed using a numeric identifier or lexical label

A method of organization according to a set of pre-established principles, usually characterized by a notation system and a hierarchical structure of relationships among the entities. Defines structure and organization of a classification including the hierarchical ranks

Terminological resource which has characteristics of mutual exclusiveness and exhaustiveness to aggregate data to a pre-prescribed level of specialization for a specific purpose. Extends the classification scheme concept to include the value domain used to populate a classification scheme
A single concept in a classification system or scheme at any hierarchical level.
A versioned instance of a classification scheme
Notes: In a version, the categories of the classification version are split, aggregated or regrouped to provide additions or alternatives to the standard order and structure of the base version.

Definition: The numeric distance of a nested level from the root of a hierarchy in a stratified classification scheme
A name sanctioned by an authoritative body (e.g. naming authority, formal classification system) based on a defined set of unambiguous criteria and belonging to a formal nomenclature
Concept system in which all concepts are related in hierarchical relations that form a partial ordering
Process of recognizing an entity in a particular domain as distinct from other entities.

A classification system for grouping both living and extinct organisms governed by the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Generally, the parent-child relationships in the Linnaean hierarchy represent the lineage evolution between species.
Hierarchical arrangement of concepts in a classification scheme in which each concept can have only one broader concept at the level immediately above.
Primary means of identification of objects and concepts for humans
Notes: The term ‘Name’ refers to any label assigned to a specimen for identification, including both terms that belong to a formal classification system and informal alternate terms.

Definition: A registration authority that allocates names according to specified rules.

Refers to any name assigned to a specimen at the object level (before atomization into constituent parts). Specimen names are often written as compound terms, a concatenation of multiple informal and formal identifiers.
The range of values used to populate a classification scheme (or classification scheme variant)
Notes: Equivalent to the range includes property of a classification system

Definition: abstraction of real world phenomena
Source: ISO 19101-1:2014(en) Geographic information — Reference model — Part 1: Fundamentals

Definition: A feature of interest is an abstraction of a real-world phenomenon \which is being sampled or transformed in an act of Sampling..
Notes: A feature of interest is defined in terms of its properties, which are qualifiable, quantifiable, observable, or operable qualities.

Definition: A physical result of a sampling (or subsampling) event. Material samples are typically collected and either preserved or destructively processed.
A natural geomorphological feature that has been created by natural Earth processes.
A natural feature of the solid surface of the Earth or other planetary body.
A feature which is intended to be representative of a `FeatureOfInterest` on which `Observations` may be made.
An activity of Sampling carries out a (Sampling) Procedure to create or transform one or more Samples.
The feature of interest a sample is intended to be representative of.
The nature of the feature such as whether the feature is the result of natural processes.
The geographic place where a sampling event takes place.

Geologic units defined or characterized on the basis of their contained fossils. Biostratigraphic units exist only where the particular diagnostic feature or attribute on which they are based has been identified.
Bodies of rocks, layered or unlayered, that are defined between specified stratigraphic horizons which represent specified intervals of geologic time.

A body of rock that persists through time, forming a discrete and definable unit. Geologic units are identified by their geometric, compositional, and internal structural characteristics, as well as their spatio-temporal relations with other rock bodies.
Notes: Geologic Units Include both formal units (i.e. formally adopted and named in an official lexicon) and informal units (i.e. named but not promoted to the lexicon) and unnamed units (i.e. recognisable and described and delineable in the field but not otherwise formalised).

Definition: A scheme that specifies concepts used to categorize types of geologic units. Unit types are differentiated based on their defining composition, temporal context, or other physical properties.
A general law upon which all geologic chronology is based, where younger lithostratigraphic units lie atop older lithostratigraphic units
Notes: In any sequence of layered rocks, sedimentary or extrusive volcanic, that has not been overturned, the youngest stratum is at the top and the oldest at the base; i.e., each bed is younger that the bed beneath, but older than the bed above it

Definition: A defined body of predominantly intrusive, highly deformed, and (or) highly metamorphosed rock, distinguished and delimited based on rock characteristics
Notes: Lithodemic units do not follow the law of superposition.

Definition: (a) The description of rocks, especially in hand specimens and outcrops, based on characteristics such as color, mineralogic composition, and grain size. (b) The physical character of a rock.
A defined body of sedimentary, extrusive igneous, metasedimentary, or metavolcanic strata that is distinguished and delimited based on lithic characteristics and stratigraphic position
Notes: Lithostratigraphic units obey the law of superposition.

Definition: Bodies of rock strata unified by similar magnetic characteristics which allow them to be differentiated from adjacent strata.
A lithologic variant in a sedimentary unit, typically related to spatial variation in the original depositional environment or subsequent diagenetic environment.

(a) A composite diagram that shows in a single column the subdivisions of part or all of geologic time or the sequence of stratigraphic units of a given locality or region (the oldest at the bottom and the youngest at the top, with dips adjusted to the horizontal) so arranged as to indicate their relations to the subdivisions of geologic time and their relative positions to each other (b) The vertical or chronologic arrangement or sequence of rock units portrayed in a geologic column.

A body of rock established as a distinct entity in the classification of the rocks, based on any of the properties or attributes or combinations thereof that rocks possess.International Stratigraphic Guide

The description of all rock bodies forming the Earth’s crust and their organization into distinctive, useful, mappable units based on their inherent properties or attributes in order to establish their distribution and relationship in space and their succession in time, and to interpret geologic history.
Geologic unit defined on basis of structural or deformation features, mutual relations, origin or historical evolution. Contained material may be igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic.
Notes: Concept referred to as a lithotectonic unit in source

Definition: Sequence of characters permanently associated with an object or aspect of an object for reference to uniquely identify it in a specified context
